title: Monumenta Vetera ad Donatistarum Historiam Pertinentia
author: AA VV
source: Translated by Claude from tmp87.tmp87.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Praeterea cum hinc, sicut ex historia passionis sanctorum Saturnini et Dativi, et ex actis purgationis Felicis episcopi Aptungitani et Caeciliani Garthaginensis, intelligamus originem tra- ditorum, quo nomine nihil aut vulgatius, aut contu- meliosius fuit in Ecclesia Africana, peit ex initio persecutionis quam describit Lactantius, officii nostri esse arbitrati sumus cum ille conjungere vetera illius aevi monumenta sincera quae reperiri possent, emen- data ex fide veterum exemplarium.
passages.english: Moreover, since from this source, namely from the history of the passion of Saints Saturninus and Dativus and from the acts of the clearing of Felix, bishop of Abthugni, and of Caecilian of Carthage, we understand the origin of the *traditores* [those who handed over the scriptures], a name than which nothing was either more common or more insulting in the African Church, [and which] arose from the beginning of the persecution which Lactantius describes, we have judged it to be our duty to join with it the genuine ancient documents of that age which could be found, corrected on the authority of the old copies.
passages.notes: "peit" is evidently a scanning error, probably for "petitam" or "profluxit" or similar; translated as "arose". "cum ille" read as "cum illo" (with it, i.e. Lactantius' work). "Garthaginensis" read as "Carthaginensis".

passages.original: His actis usi sunt catholici adversus Donatistas, ut ostende- rent etiam tempore persecutionis concilium duodecim episcoporum congregari potuisse, quandoquidem tunc Christiani collectas et sacros conventus celebra- verant. Id refert Augustinus in Breviculo collationis dic 3, cap. 17 : Catholici, inquit, respondebant mul- to facilius duodecim homines in domum convenire po-tuisse eo tempore, quo etiam congregationes plebium fieri solebant, quamvis persecutione soeviente, sicut ip- sis gestis martyrum monstrabatur, qui confitebantur in passionibus suis se collectam et dominicum egisse.
passages.english: The Catholics used these acts against the Donatists, to show that even in a time of persecution a council of twelve bishops could have been gathered, since at that time the Christians had held assemblies and sacred meetings. Augustine reports this in the Breviculus of the Conference, day 3, chapter 17: "The Catholics," he says, "replied that twelve men could much more easily have met in a house at a time when even gatherings of the common people used to take place, although the persecution was raging, as was shown by the very acts of the martyrs, who confessed in their passions that they had held the assembly and the Lord's [service]."
passages.notes: "dic 3" read as "die 3". "dominicum" refers to the Lord's supper/Sunday service.

passages.original: IV. Porro plures etiam martyres in Numidia occa- sione sacrorum librorum occubuisse discimus ex re- scriptis Secundi Tigisitani episcopi ad Mensurium Car- thaginensem, ubi. teste sancto Augustino in Brevi- culo collationis die 3, cap. 13. Secundus narrat in Numidia persecutores quoe egerint, et qui comprehensi, et Scripturas sanctas tradere nolentes, et multa mala passi, et gravissimis suppliciis excruciati et occisi sunt. Haec sub Floro contigere, quem Numidioe persecuto- rem appellat Optatus lib. iii ad Parmenianum.
passages.english: IV. Further, we learn that several more martyrs also died in Numidia on account of the sacred books, from the letters of Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, to Mensurius of Carthage, in which, as Saint Augustine attests in the Breviculus of the Conference, day 3, chapter 13, Secundus relates what the persecutors did in Numidia, and who were arrested and, refusing to hand over the holy Scriptures, both suffered many evils and were tortured with the most severe punishments and killed. These things happened under Florus, whom Optatus, book 3 against Parmenian, calls the persecutor of Numidia.

passages.original: In indice Collationis Carthag. 3, cap. 516, legitur, Recitatio judicii Constantini, quo apud se quoque Caecilianum fuisse purgatum post Arelatense Concilium significat Imperator. Ibid., cap. 521. Interlocutio quod inter partes sententiam tulerit Imperator. Ibid., cap. 523 : Interlocutio hoc ipsum significans ex rescripto Principis superius recitato. Rescriptum istud ad Eu- malium vicarium Africae, laudat Augustinus in Bre- viculo Collat. III, n. 37; et lib. post Collationem, n. 56, ubi datum dicit Sabino et Ruffino consulibus, quarto idus novembres (1). Ipsam quoque Constantini sententiam secundum Caecilianum dictam ex eodem rescripto affert in lib. III contra Crescon., n. 82 : Insero adhuc, ait, et verba Constantini ex litteris ejus ad Eumalium vicarium, ubi se inter partes cognovisse, et innocentem Caecilianum comperisse testatur.
passages.english: In the index of the Conference of Carthage, [day] 3, chapter 516, one reads: "The reading of the judgment of Constantine, in which the Emperor indicates that Caecilian had been cleared before him too, after the Council of Arles." Ibid., chapter 521: "Interlocution [stating] that the Emperor had given judgment between the parties." Ibid., chapter 523: "Interlocution indicating this very thing from the rescript of the Emperor read out above." Augustine cites this rescript to Eumalius, vicar of Africa, in the Breviculus of the Conference III, no. 37, and in the book after the Conference, no. 56, where he says it was issued in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus, on the fourth day before the Ides of November (1). He also adduces Constantine's actual sentence, pronounced in favour of Caecilian, from the same rescript in book III against Cresconius, no. 82: "I insert further," he says, "also the words of Constantine from his letter to the vicar Eumalius, where he testifies that he heard [the case] between the parties and found Caecilian innocent."
passages.notes: "(1)" is a footnote reference in the edition. The date corresponds to 10 November 316.

passages.original: 50 et 51 : Ab operariis uni- tatis multa quidem aspere gesta sunt, sed ea quid im- putatis Leontio, Macario, vel Taurino? et eodem in libro § X, p. 66 et 67 : Displicent vobis tempora, nes- cio cujus, Leontii, Ursatii, Macarii et caeterorum Fuit primo tempestas sub Ursatio secula est pluvia sub Gregorio post pluviam secuti sunt lapides sub Operariis unitatis, Cresconius apud Augustinum dicit Silvanum Cirtensem communicare noluisse Ursatio et Zenophilo persequentibus, et ideo actum esse in exilium. Petilianus quoque Donatista commemorans eos comites qui Donatistis infensi fuerant, Ursatium inter eos commemorat : Periit, inquit, Macarius : periit Ursatius, cunctique comites vestri.
passages.english: 50 and 51: "Many harsh things were indeed done by the workers of unity, but why do you impute them to Leontius, Macarius, or Taurinus?" And in the same book, § X, pp. 66 and 67: "You are displeased with the times of, I know not whom, Leontius, Ursatius, Macarius and the rest. First there was a storm under Ursatius; rain followed under Gregory; after the rain came stones under the workers of unity." Cresconius, as cited by Augustine, says that Silvanus of Cirta refused to communicate with Ursatius and Zenophilus when they were persecuting, and was therefore driven into exile. Petilian the Donatist too, recalling those counts who had been hostile to the Donatists, mentions Ursatius among them: "Macarius perished," he says, "Ursatius perished, and all your counts."
passages.notes: Passage begins mid-reference (Optatus book III §1, pp. 50–51). "secula" read as "secuta". Punctuation of the quotations is uncertain in the scanned text.

passages.original: Catholici apud Augustinum sub finem tractatus II in Joannem negant Marculum a se praecipitatum, sed se ipsum praecipitem egisse dicunt : « Proferunt Do- natistae nobis nescio quos in persecutione suas mar- tyres. Ecce Marculus de petra praecipitatus est : ecce Donatus Bagaiensis in puteum missus est.
passages.english: The Catholics, as cited by Augustine toward the end of Tractate II on John, deny that Marculus was thrown down by them, but say that he threw himself headlong: "The Donatists bring forward to us some martyrs of theirs, I know not who, in the persecution. 'Look, Marculus was thrown down from a rock; look, Donatus of Bagai was cast into a well.'
